stem: The uppermost portion of the iliac crest is at about the level of
explanation: The top of the iliac crest lies at about L4–L5, a common centering landmark for the abdomen and lumbar spine.

stem: The AP shoulder in external rotation places which structure in profile laterally?
explanation: External rotation is the true AP position: the greater tubercle is in profile laterally and the lesser tubercle lies anteriorly.

stem: Internal rotation of the arm, with the epicondyles perpendicular to the IR, places in profile the
explanation: Internal rotation gives a lateral humerus, showing the lesser tubercle in profile medially.

stem: When a trauma patient cannot abduct the arm, a lateral of the proximal humerus is obtained with the
explanation: The transthoracic lateral shows the glenohumeral joint and upper humerus without moving the arm.

stem: The inferosuperior axial projection of the shoulder requires that the patient
options: be able to abduct the arm
keep the arm at the side
explanation: The arm must be abducted so the beam can pass up through the axilla; patients who cannot abduct need a transthoracic lateral.

stem: The tangential projection of the wrist (Gaynor-Hart method) demonstrates the
explanation: The Gaynor-Hart tangential projection looks down the carpal canal and is used to detect carpal canal defects.

stem: With the elbow flexed 90 degrees and the central ray angled 45 degrees toward the shoulder, the projection shows the
options: joint space between the radial head and capitulum
explanation: This trauma axial lateral (Coyle method) opens the radiocapitellar joint when the patient cannot extend the arm.

stem: The capitulum of the humerus articulates with the
explanation: The capitulum, lateral to the trochlea, articulates with the head of the radius.

stem: Which projection of the foot best shows the cuboid, the sinus tarsi and the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal?
options: Medial oblique, plantar surface 30 degrees to the IR
AP with the central ray 10 degrees posteriorly
explanation: The medial oblique opens most of the tarsals and intertarsal spaces, including the cuboid and sinus tarsi.

stem: Which projection of the foot shows the spaces between the first and second metatarsals and between the first and second cuneiforms?
explanation: The lateral oblique opens the medial interspaces that the medial oblique closes.

stem: Turning the foot outward at the ankle is called
explanation: Eversion turns the sole outward; inversion turns it inward.

stem: The posterior oblique projection of the acetabulum (Judet method) requires an obliquity of the midsagittal plane of
explanation: The Judet method rotates the whole body 45 degrees to show the acetabular rim and columns.

stem: For an AP projection of the sacrum, the central ray is directed
explanation: A 15-degree cephalad angle, centered midway between the pubic symphysis and the ASIS, matches the sacrum's tilt.

stem: For an AP projection of the coccyx, the central ray is directed
explanation: The coccyx curves forward, so the central ray is angled 10 degrees caudad, centered about 2 in above the pubic symphysis.

stem: The articular facets of L5–S1 are best demonstrated in a
explanation: The L5–S1 facets lie at a smaller angle to the midsagittal plane than the upper lumbar facets, so a 30-degree oblique opens them.

stem: The thoracic zygapophyseal joints are demonstrated in an oblique position with the
options: coronal plane 30 degrees to the IR
coronal plane 70 degrees to the IR
explanation: The thoracic facets lie 70 degrees to the MSP, so the patient is turned 20 degrees from lateral: coronal plane 70 degrees to the IR.

stem: The thoracic intervertebral foramina are best demonstrated in the
explanation: The thoracic intervertebral foramina are 90 degrees to the MSP, so they are seen in the lateral.

stem: A breathing technique for a lateral thoracic spine is used to
options: blur the overlying lung markings and ribs with a long exposure time
explanation: An exposure long enough to cover a few breaths, with low mA, blurs the lung markings while the spine stays still.

stem: For a lateral projection of the skull, the interpupillary line is placed
explanation: With the interpupillary line perpendicular and the MSP parallel to the IR, the skull is in a true lateral.

stem: The parietoorbital projection (Rhese method), with the zygoma, nose and chin touching the IR, demonstrates the
explanation: The three-point landing of the Rhese method shows the optic foramen (canal) end-on.

stem: A depressed zygomatic arch may be demonstrated by modifying which projection?
explanation: Rotating the head slightly in the SMV projects the arch free of the skull, even when it is depressed or the cheekbones are flat.

stem: In a patient with a hypersthenic body habitus, the stomach usually lies
explanation: Hypersthenic patients have a short, wide trunk with a high, transverse stomach.

stem: In the PA projection of a hypersthenic stomach, which central ray angle opens up the stomach?
explanation: A 35- to 45-degree cephalad angle projects the overlapping parts of the high transverse stomach apart.

stem: During myelography, contrast is introduced into the
explanation: Myelography uses an intrathecal injection into the subarachnoid space around the spinal cord.

stem: In ERCP, contrast is introduced through a cannula placed in the
explanation: An endoscope is passed into the duodenum, and the hepatopancreatic ampulla is cannulated to fill the ducts.

stem: ERCP is performed to investigate the
explanation: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography images the bile ducts and the pancreatic duct.

stem: Which position moves the gallbladder away from the spine?
explanation: The LAO position (or a right lateral decubitus) moves the gallbladder away from the vertebral column.

stem: The capitulum of the humerus lies
explanation: The capitulum is on the lateral side of the distal humerus, beside the trochlea.

stem: To show the radial head free of the ulna in an oblique elbow, the arm is rotated
explanation: The lateral oblique separates the radial head and neck from the ulna; the medial oblique shows the coronoid process.

stem: A patient cannot fully extend the elbow. The AP elbow is then taken as
options: one projection through the forearm only
two projections: one with the humerus and one with the forearm parallel to the IR
explanation: With partial flexion, two APs are made, one for the distal humerus and one for the proximal forearm, each parallel to the IR.

stem: The lateral projection of the elbow, flexed 90 degrees, demonstrates which structure in profile?
options: Radial head, free of the ulna
explanation: The lateral elbow shows the olecranon process in profile; the lateral oblique frees the radial head and the medial oblique shows the coronoid.

stem: Which vertebral curves are primary curves, present at birth?
explanation: The thoracic and sacral curves are kyphotic, primary curves; the cervical and lumbar lordotic curves develop after birth.

stem: The cervical and lumbar curves of the spine are
explanation: They are lordotic and develop after birth, as the child holds up the head and begins to walk.

stem: For an AP lumbar spine, the patient's knees are flexed to
options: decrease the lordotic curve, bringing the back closer to the table
explanation: Flexing the knees flattens the lumbar curve so the spine lies closer to the IR and the disk spaces open.

stem: The PA oblique projection of the wrist (lateral rotation, 45 degrees) best demonstrates the
explanation: Lateral rotation shows the carpals on the lateral (thumb) side: the trapezium and scaphoid.

stem: The pisiform is best demonstrated free of the other carpals in which projection?
explanation: The AP oblique in medial rotation shows the pisiform and the medial carpals.

stem: In the lateral projection of the ankle, the foot is dorsiflexed to better demonstrate the
explanation: With the tibia and fibula superimposed and the foot dorsiflexed, the talotibial joint is shown best.

stem: For an AP supine abdomen (KUB), the central ray is usually centered at the level of the
explanation: Centering at the iliac crests includes the kidneys and the bladder on one receptor for most patients.

stem: In the LPO position during an upper GI series, barium fills the
explanation: Barium sinks to the posterior fundus in the LPO, while air rises into the body, antrum and duodenal bulb for double contrast.

stem: A small bowel series is complete when barium reaches the
explanation: Images are taken until contrast passes the ileocecal valve into the large bowel.

stem: Which projection is used especially for the rectum during a barium enema?
explanation: The lateral shows the rectum and rectosigmoid in profile.

stem: During a barium enema, the LAO (and RPO) position best demonstrates the
explanation: The LAO opens the splenic flexure; the RAO and LPO open the hepatic flexure.

stem: In cystography, contrast is introduced into the bladder
explanation: A retrograde cystogram fills the bladder through a catheter in the urethra.

stem: Which study shows the urethra while the patient voids?
explanation: A voiding cystourethrogram images the bladder and urethra during urination.

stem: Arthrography evaluates which type of joint?
explanation: Contrast is injected into the capsule of a freely movable synovial joint, such as the shoulder or knee.

stem: During lower-limb venography, tourniquets above the knee and ankle are used to fill the
explanation: The tourniquets suppress superficial filling and force contrast into the deep veins.

stem: The coronoid process is located on the
explanation: The coronoid process projects from the front of the proximal ulna; the olecranon is at the back.

stem: A decubitus position is one in which the patient is
options: lying down, with a horizontal x-ray beam
explanation: Decubitus means lying down; the projection is made with a horizontal beam to show air or fluid levels.

stem: The dens (odontoid process) is part of
explanation: The dens projects up from the body of C2 and forms a pivot joint with C1.

stem: To demonstrate the right axillary ribs in an AP oblique projection, the patient is placed in which position?
explanation: AP obliques show the axillary ribs on the side nearer the IR, so the right side needs an RPO.
